body.en:
A tree is a non-linear data structure that stores data in a hierarchical (parent–child) form.

Definition: a tree is a finite set of one or more nodes such that:

  1. there is one specially designated node called the root, and
  2. the remaining nodes are divided into n ≥ 0 disjoint sets T1, T2, …, Tn, each of which is itself a tree, called a subtree of the root.

This definition is recursive: a tree is made of smaller trees.

General tree

A general tree is a tree in which a node can have any number of children (0, 1, 2, 3, …). Example: the folder structure of a computer, an organisation chart, a family tree.

Properties

  • There is exactly one path between the root and any node.
  • A tree with n nodes has exactly n − 1 edges.
  • A tree has no cycle.

Linear vs non-linear

In arrays, stacks, queues and linked lists, each element has one next element (linear). In a tree, one node can have many next nodes (children), so it is non-linear.

The examples refer to the tree in the "Tree: Basic Terminology" diagram: A has children B, C, D; B has E, F; F has J; D has G, H, I.

TermMeaningExample
Nodean element of the tree holding dataA, B, …, J (10 nodes)
Root nodethe topmost node; it has no parentA
Edgethe link between a parent and a childA–B (9 edges)

Note: some books start levels at 1 and count height in levels (then the height here is 4). In the exam, state the convention you use.

A forest is a set of n ≥ 0 disjoint trees.

  • If the root of a tree is deleted, its subtrees form a forest.
  • Conversely, if a new node is added as the parent of the roots of all trees in a forest, we get a single tree.
  • Example: deleting root R from a tree whose children are B, C, D gives a forest of 3 trees rooted at B, C and D.
  • A forest can also be converted into one binary tree: convert each tree into a binary tree, then join the roots as right siblings.

h.en: 4.1.4 Binary Tree, Strict Binary Tree and Complete Binary Tree

body.en:
Binary tree

A binary tree is a tree in which every node has at most two children, called the left child and the right child. (A binary tree may also be empty.) The order matters: a node with only a left child is different from a node with only a right child.

Strict binary tree

A binary tree in which every non-leaf node has exactly two children (each node has 0 or 2 children). A strict binary tree with n leaves always has 2n − 1 nodes.

Complete binary tree

A binary tree in which all levels are completely filled except possibly the last level, and the nodes of the last level are placed as far left as possible. Complete binary trees are used for heaps and can be stored easily in an array.

(A full / perfect binary tree has all levels completely filled: 2h+1 − 1 nodes.)

Properties of a binary tree

  • Maximum number of nodes at level l = 2l (root at level 0).
  • Maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height h = 2h+1 − 1.
  • Minimum height of a binary tree with n nodes = ⌊log2 n⌋.
  • Number of leaves = number of nodes with two children + 1.

Linked representation

Each node of a binary tree is a structure with three fields: a pointer to the left child, the data, and a pointer to the right child.

struct tnode {
    struct tnode *left;
    int data;
    struct tnode *right;
};
  • A pointer root holds the address of the root node; root = NULL means the tree is empty.
  • A missing child is shown by a NULL pointer; leaf nodes have both pointers NULL.
  • Nodes are created dynamically with malloc, so the tree can grow as needed.

Array (sequential) representation

  • The root is stored at index 0. For a node at index i, the left child is at 2i + 1 and the right child at 2i + 2; the parent is at ⌊(i − 1)/2⌋.
  • It suits complete binary trees; for other trees many array places stay empty (memory waste).

h.en: 4.1.6 Conversion of a General Tree to a Binary Tree

body.en:
A general tree can have any number of children, which is hard to store. It is converted to a binary tree using the left child – right sibling method.

Conversion: General -> Binary
Step 1: Keep the root as it is.
Step 2: For every node, its leftmost
        (first) child becomes its
        LEFT child.
Step 3: Its next sibling (immediate
        right brother) becomes its
        RIGHT child.
Step 4: Delete all other links from
        parent to children.

Example

General tree: A has children B, C, D; B has E, F; D has G, H.

  • A: left = B (first child), right = none (the root has no sibling).
  • B: left = E, right = C. C: right = D.
  • E: right = F. D: left = G. G: right = H.

In the binary tree, a left link means "first child" and a right link means "next sibling". The preorder of the binary tree is the same as the preorder of the general tree (A B E F C D G H). The root of the converted tree never has a right child.

Traversal means visiting every node of a tree exactly once in a fixed order. A binary tree has three standard (depth-first) traversals, named by when the root (N) is visited.

1. Inorder (Left – Node – Right)

Algorithm INORDER(T)
Step 1: If T != NULL then
          INORDER(LEFT(T))
          Visit INFO(T)
          INORDER(RIGHT(T))
Step 2: Exit

2. Preorder (Node – Left – Right)

Algorithm PREORDER(T)
Step 1: If T != NULL then
          Visit INFO(T)
          PREORDER(LEFT(T))
          PREORDER(RIGHT(T))
Step 2: Exit

3. Postorder (Left – Right – Node)

Algorithm POSTORDER(T)
Step 1: If T != NULL then
          POSTORDER(LEFT(T))
          POSTORDER(RIGHT(T))
          Visit INFO(T)
Step 2: Exit

Example (tree in the diagram)

TraversalOrderResult
InorderL N RD B G E A C F
PreorderN L RA B D E G C F
PostorderL R ND G E B F C A

Points to remember

  • In preorder the root is first; in postorder the root is last.
  • The inorder traversal of a BST gives the data in ascending order.
  • For an expression tree, inorder gives the infix, preorder the prefix and postorder the postfix expression.
  • Each traversal takes O(n) time. Recursion uses the system stack.

Easy trick

Go round the tree anticlockwise starting from the left of the root. Write a node when you pass its left side (preorder), its bottom (inorder) or its right side (postorder).

h.en: 4.2.2 Constructing a Binary Tree from Traversals

body.en:
A unique binary tree can be built from inorder + preorder or from inorder + postorder. (Preorder + postorder alone is not enough.)

Method (inorder + preorder)

  1. The first value of the preorder is the root.
  2. Find the root in the inorder: values on its left form the left subtree; values on its right form the right subtree.
  3. Repeat for each subtree with the next values of the preorder.

With postorder, the last value is the root, and the subtrees are built right first, then left.

h.en: 4.3.1 Binary Search Tree: Definition and Construction

body.en:
A binary search tree is a binary tree in which, for every node:

  • all values in its left subtree are less than the node's value,
  • all values in its right subtree are greater than the node's value, and
  • the left and right subtrees are also binary search trees.

Duplicate values are normally not allowed.

Construction

Insert the values one by one. The first value becomes the root. For each next value, start at the root and move left if smaller, right if larger, until an empty (NULL) place is found; the new node is placed there as a leaf.

Example: insert 45, 25, 65, 15, 35, 55, 75, 30.

  • 45 is the root. 25 < 45 → left. 65 > 45 → right.
  • 15 → left of 25. 35 → right of 25. 55 → left of 65. 75 → right of 65.
  • 30: 30 < 45 left, 30 > 25 right, 30 < 35 left → left child of 35.
  • Inorder: 15 25 30 35 45 55 65 75 (sorted).

Advantages

  • Searching, insertion and deletion take O(h) time: O(log n) for a balanced tree.
  • Inorder traversal gives sorted data.
  • Disadvantage: if the data is inserted in sorted order, the BST becomes skewed (like a linked list) and operations become O(n).

h.en: 4.3.2 Insertion of a Node in a BST

body.en:
Algorithm BSTINSERT(ROOT, ITEM)
Step 1: [Create node]
        NEW = getnode()
        INFO(NEW) = ITEM
        LEFT(NEW) = RIGHT(NEW) = NULL
Step 2: If ROOT = NULL then
          Set ROOT = NEW and Exit
Step 3: Set PTR = ROOT
Step 4: Repeat
          If ITEM < INFO(PTR) then
            If LEFT(PTR) = NULL then
              LEFT(PTR) = NEW, Exit
            Else PTR = LEFT(PTR)
          Else If ITEM > INFO(PTR) then
            If RIGHT(PTR) = NULL then
              RIGHT(PTR) = NEW, Exit
            Else PTR = RIGHT(PTR)
          Else
            Write "Duplicate", Exit

Recursive C function

struct tnode *insert(struct tnode *t,
                     int x)
{
    if (t == NULL) {
        t = malloc(sizeof(struct tnode));
        t->data = x;
        t->left = t->right = NULL;
    } else if (x < t->data)
        t->left = insert(t->left, x);
    else if (x > t->data)
        t->right = insert(t->right, x);
    return t;
}
  • A new node is always inserted as a leaf.
  • The path followed is the same path a search for that value would follow.
  • Time: O(h).

h.en: 4.3.3 Searching a Node in a BST

body.en:
Compare the item with the root. If equal, the search is successful. If smaller, search only the left subtree; if larger, search only the right subtree. Half of the remaining tree is skipped at each step (like binary search).

Algorithm BSTSEARCH(ROOT, ITEM)
Step 1: Set PTR = ROOT
Step 2: Repeat while PTR != NULL
          If ITEM = INFO(PTR) then
            Write "Found" and Exit
          Else If ITEM < INFO(PTR) then
            Set PTR = LEFT(PTR)
          Else
            Set PTR = RIGHT(PTR)
Step 3: Write "Not found"
Step 4: Exit
  • Example: search 30 → 45, 25, 35, 30: found in 4 comparisons.
  • Search 60 → 45, 65, 55, then the right of 55 is NULL: not found.
  • The minimum value is the leftmost node and the maximum is the rightmost node.
  • Time: best O(1), average O(log n), worst O(n) (skewed tree).

h.en: 4.3.4 Deletion of a Node from a BST

body.en:
After deletion the tree must still be a BST. There are three cases:

Case 1: the node is a leaf

Simply remove it: the parent's link becomes NULL. Example: delete 15.

Case 2: the node has one child

Connect the parent directly to the node's only child, then remove the node. Example: delete 35 (child 30) → 30 takes the place of 35.

Case 3: the node has two children

Replace the node's value with its inorder successor (the smallest value in its right subtree: go right once, then left as far as possible), and then delete the successor (which is case 1 or 2). Example: delete 25 → successor 30 replaces 25.

(The inorder predecessor, the largest value in the left subtree, can be used instead.)

Algorithm BSTDELETE(ROOT, ITEM)
Step 1: Search ITEM; let PTR be the
        node and PAR its parent.
        If not found: Write "Not
        found" and Exit
Step 2: [Case 1: leaf]
        If PTR has no child then
          set PAR's link to NULL
Step 3: [Case 2: one child]
        If PTR has one child then
          set PAR's link to that child
Step 4: [Case 3: two children]
        Find SUC = inorder successor
        (leftmost node of RIGHT(PTR))
        INFO(PTR) = INFO(SUC)
        Delete SUC (case 1 or 2)
Step 5: Free the removed node, Exit

h.en: 4.3.5 Complete BST Program and Applications of Trees

body.en:
The menu-driven program below combines insert, search, delete and the three traversals.

Applications of trees

  • BST: fast searching, sorting (inorder) and dictionaries.
  • File systems and folder hierarchy (general tree).
  • Expression trees in compilers (infix, prefix, postfix).
  • Database indexing (B-trees), heaps for priority queues.
  • Decision trees, game trees, organisation charts.
  • Huffman coding trees for data compression.

A graph G = (V, E) is a non-linear data structure that consists of a set of vertices V and a set of edges E, where each edge connects a pair of vertices.

TermMeaning
Vertex (node)a point of the graph that stores data, e.g. A, B, C
Edge (arc)a line joining two vertices, written (A, B)
Adjacent verticestwo vertices joined by an edge
Degreenumber of edges connected to a vertex (undirected graph)
In-degree / Out-degreenumber of edges coming into / going out of a vertex (directed graph)
Patha sequence of vertices in which each consecutive pair is joined by an edge, e.g. A–B–E–C
Cyclea path that starts and ends at the same vertex with no edge repeated, e.g. B–D–E–B
Isolated vertexa vertex with degree 0
Self-loopan edge from a vertex to itself

In an undirected graph, the sum of the degrees of all vertices = 2 × number of edges.

1. Undirected graph: edges have no direction; (A, B) is the same as (B, A). Example: a road with two-way traffic.
  2. Directed graph (digraph): every edge has a direction, shown by an arrow; <A, B> goes from A to B only. Example: one-way roads, links between web pages.
  3. Connected graph: there is a path between every pair of vertices. If not, it is a disconnected graph.
  4. Complete graph: every vertex is joined to every other vertex. An undirected complete graph with n vertices has n(n − 1)/2 edges (written Kn). A complete digraph has n(n − 1) edges.
  5. Weighted graph: every edge has a value (weight) such as distance, cost or time. Example: a road map with distances.

Other types: a cyclic graph contains a cycle; an acyclic graph does not. A tree is a connected acyclic graph.

1. Adjacency matrix

A 2-D array adj[n][n] where adj[i][j] = 1 if there is an edge from i to j, else 0. For a weighted graph the weight is stored. It is symmetric for an undirected graph. Memory: O(n²).

2. Adjacency list

An array of linked lists: list i contains all vertices adjacent to vertex i. It uses memory only for existing edges, O(n + e), so it suits sparse graphs.

Tree vs graph

TreeGraph
Hierarchical structureNetwork structure
Has one root nodeNo root node
No cyclesMay contain cycles
n nodes → exactly n − 1 edgesAny number of edges
Exactly one path between two nodesOne or more paths
Traversal: inorder, preorder, postorderTraversal: BFS, DFS
e.g. folder structuree.g. road map, social network

Applications of graphs

  • Maps and GPS shortest routes, computer networks, social networks (friends), web page links, airline routes, project scheduling.

expl.en:
• Each tree node has a left pointer, data and a right pointer (linked representation).
  • The tree built is the one in the traversal diagram: A(B(D, E(G)), C(–, F)).
  • All three functions are recursive: the answer for a tree = the answer for its left subtree + right subtree (+ the node itself).
  • Leaves are D, G and F. Height = 3 edges (A → B → E → G).

programs.out:
Inorder  : D B G E A C F 
Preorder : A B D E G C F 
Postorder: D G E B F C A

expl.en:
• Inorder (L N R): left subtree, node, right subtree.
  • Preorder (N L R): node first; the root is always the first value.
  • Postorder (L R N): node last; the root is always the last value.
  • The three functions differ only in where the printf is placed. The recursion stops at NULL.

title.en: Construct a Binary Search Tree and display it [Practical 10]

expl.en:
• BST rule: smaller values go to the left subtree and larger values to the right.
  • insert() is recursive: it moves left or right until it finds a NULL place and creates the new node there.
  • Duplicates are not inserted (the second 35 is rejected).
  • The inorder traversal of a BST always gives the values in ascending order.

title.en: Search a value in a BST (shows the path)

programs.out:
Search 30: 45 25 35 30 FOUND, 4 steps
Search 75: 45 65 75 FOUND, 3 steps
Search 60: 45 65 55 NOT FOUND, 3 steps

expl.en:
• At each node: if x is equal → found; if smaller → go left; if larger → go right.
  • Only one path from the root is checked, so a search takes O(h) comparisons (h = height), not O(n).
  • 60 is not found: 60 > 45 → right, 60 < 65 → left, 60 > 55 → right is NULL.

title.en: Delete a node from a BST (all three cases)

expl.en:
• Case 1, leaf: the node is simply removed (its parent's pointer becomes NULL).
  • Case 2, one child: the child takes the place of the deleted node (35 is replaced by 30).
  • Case 3, two children: copy the inorder successor (the smallest value in the right subtree) into the node, then delete the successor. Deleting the root 45 makes 55 the new root.
  • Inorder is still sorted after every deletion, which proves the BST property is kept. The preorder shows the new shape.

title.en: Find the minimum and maximum in a BST

expl.en:
• The smallest value is the leftmost node: keep going left until left is NULL.
  • The largest value is the rightmost node.
  • No comparisons with data are needed; the BST shape itself gives the answer in O(h).

expl.en:
• The three graphs are the Connected, Disconnected and Complete (K4) panels of the "Types of Graph" diagram.
  • Connected: starting from vertex A, a depth-first visit reaches every vertex.
  • Complete: every pair of vertices is joined, so the edges = n(n − 1)/2 = 6 for n = 4.

• Each vertex has a linked list of its adjacent vertices (an application of Unit 3).
  • New neighbours are inserted at the beginning of the list (O(1)), so they appear in reverse order of input.
  • An adjacency list uses memory only for the existing edges, so it is better than a matrix for sparse graphs.

q.en: What is a tree?

a.en: A non-linear hierarchical data structure of nodes with one root, in which every other node has exactly one parent.

q.en: What is a root node?

a.en: The topmost node of a tree; it has no parent.

q.en: What is a leaf node?

a.en: A node with no children (degree 0).

q.en: What are siblings?

a.en: Nodes having the same parent.

q.en: What is the degree of a node?

a.en: The number of children (subtrees) of that node.

q.en: What is the in-degree of the root?

a.en: Zero; every other node in a tree has in-degree 1.

q.en: Define height and depth.

a.en: Depth of a node = length of the path from the root to it; height = length of the longest path from it down to a leaf.

q.en: How many edges does a tree with n nodes have?
What is a forest?

a.en: A set of disjoint trees; removing the root of a tree gives a forest.

q.en: What is a binary tree?

a.en: A tree in which every node has at most two children: left and right.

q.en: What is a strict binary tree?

a.en: A binary tree in which every node has 0 or 2 children.

q.en: What is a complete binary tree?

a.en: All levels are full except possibly the last, which is filled from the left.

q.en: Maximum nodes in a binary tree of height h?
How is a general tree converted to a binary tree?

a.en: First child becomes the left child and the next sibling becomes the right child.

q.en: What is tree traversal?

a.en: Visiting every node exactly once in a fixed order.

q.en: Give the order of the three traversals.

a.en: Inorder L N R, preorder N L R, postorder L R N.

q.en: Which traversal gives the root first and which last?

a.en: Preorder gives it first; postorder gives it last.

q.en: Which traversals are needed to build a unique tree?

a.en: Inorder with preorder, or inorder with postorder.

q.en: What is a BST?

a.en: A binary tree where left subtree values are smaller and right subtree values are larger than the node, for every node.

q.en: Which traversal of a BST gives sorted output?

a.en: Inorder.

q.en: Where is a new node inserted in a BST?

a.en: Always as a leaf, at the NULL position reached by the search path.

q.en: Where are the minimum and maximum in a BST?

a.en: Minimum is the leftmost node; maximum is the rightmost node.

q.en: What are the cases of BST deletion?

a.en: Leaf node, node with one child, node with two children.

q.en: What is the inorder successor?

a.en: The smallest node in the right subtree: go right once, then left as far as possible.

q.en: What is the time complexity of BST search?

a.en: O(h): O(log n) when balanced, O(n) when skewed.

q.en: What is a graph?

a.en: A non-linear structure G = (V, E) of vertices and edges connecting them.

q.en: Difference between directed and undirected graph?

a.en: Directed edges have a direction (arrow); undirected edges work both ways.

q.en: What is a path and a cycle?

a.en: A path is a sequence of connected vertices; a cycle is a path that starts and ends at the same vertex.

q.en: What is a complete graph?

a.en: A graph in which every vertex is connected to every other vertex; it has n(n−1)/2 edges.

q.en: What is a weighted graph?

a.en: A graph in which each edge carries a value such as distance or cost.

q.en: What is a connected graph?

a.en: A graph in which there is a path between every pair of vertices.

q.en: Name two ways to represent a graph.

a.en: Adjacency matrix and adjacency list.

q.en: Give one difference between tree and graph.

a.en: A tree has a root and no cycles; a graph has no root and may have cycles.
